extracted.intended_audience: general educated readership; teachers, social critics, and policymakers interested in education, gender, and social reform
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay diagnosing perceived modern errors about women, heredity, environment, and especially education; it offers prescriptive principles about what education is and how it ought to be conducted. The text addresses educators, reformers, and the lay public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance: by a rule or by a ruler
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only two ways of governing: by a rule and by a ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue about female political power: the author contends that 'old powers are purely personal and therefore female' and that a woman's proper sphere may require personal/autocratic freedom rather than impersonal rule (e.g., mass enfranchisement). He warns that singular charismatic figures differ from mass movements ('one Pankhurst is an exception, but a thousand Pankhursts are a nightmare').

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate suffrage by whether votes suit women, not vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is not whether women are good enough for votes: it is whether votes are good enough for women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging political reforms (like female suffrage), assess whether the institutional form (voting, parliamentary politics) fits the nature and needs of the subject, rather than assuming the subject must fit the institution. The author prefers tailored privileges or social designs over simply granting universal political rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the modern 'slave' of industrial efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern working woman bears a double burden: the grinding officialism of the office and the scrupulosity of the old home; their efficiency can be the definition of their slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not celebrate mere efficiency as emancipation; evaluate whether work conditions impose a dehumanizing, relentless regimen. Policy or reform should avoid substituting one form of domination (commerce) for another (conscience), and consider creating spaces/privileges that free women from both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid predeterministic/hereditary assumptions in policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Heredity cannot be used to predict individual character or fate; claims of moral heredity are speculative and unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational or legislative programs should not be founded on deterministic ideas about inherited traits. The author emphasizes the unpredictability of heredity ('each birth is as lonely as a miracle') and warns against legislating or educating on the basis of supposed racial or familial destinies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overclaim the directional power of environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Environment affects people but not in a single, predictable way; surroundings may produce many different outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms that assume a specific environmental input will reliably produce a specific moral or cultural output are logically weak. Use caution in asserting causal, one-directional effects from landscape, schooling, or upbringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education is transmission (tradition) not a neutral object
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no such thing as neutral education: education is the conveying of facts, views, or qualities from one generation to another and thus inherently transmits dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the idea that schools can be neutral; any teaching carries beliefs. Beware claims to 'separate dogma from education'—the author argues 'Dogma is actually the only thing that cannot be separated from education. It is education.'

rubrics_metrics.name: You cannot create by education what you have not conceived
rubrics_metrics.description: Education cannot produce ideals or values that the society has not already conceived and possessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design educational aims in light of what the community actually values and embodies; to attempt to 'create' an ideal out of thin air is futile. Prior conception and social exemplars are prerequisites for successful transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the parents/fathers if you wish to save the children
rubrics_metrics.description: It is vain to save the children if one cannot 'save' the adults; you cannot teach citizenship or virtues to children if adults do not exemplify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social policy aimed solely at children (e.g., state-run rescue or schooling) will fail unless adult society models the virtues to be taught. Emphasize strengthening the moral/social condition of adults alongside child-focused reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority is unavoidable in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether labeled 'educator' or 'instructor', the teacher exercises choice and coercion; one cannot eliminate authority from education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational philosophies that claim to avoid authority ('drawing out' the child) still impose selective development. Accept responsibility for the authoritative role and be deliberate about what faculties are encouraged or suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education is creative and necessarily coercive
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is violent because it is creative; it interferes with natural growth by shaping particular forms and purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the moral responsibility inherent in shaping young people. Framing education as benign 'self-development' obscures the real imposition involved; policy and pedagogy should openly acknowledge and ethically manage this power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer representative/traditional authority to unrepresentative innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventional authority (even when restrictive) often claims a popular mandate, while some modern innovators impose personal vetoes without representative grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating educational prohibitions or prescriptions, consider whether they express a broader social consensus or merely an individual or elite whim. The democratic basis of a rule gives it a different legitimacy than idiosyncratic reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the oldest, assured truths first to the youngest
rubrics_metrics.description: It ought to be the oldest things that are taught to the youngest people; the assured and experienced truths should be put first to the baby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum should prioritize long-tested, communal knowledge and practices before experimental or novel theories. Avoid subjecting very young learners to systems 'younger than himself' that lack rooted experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular education should mean education by the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's ideal is that Popular Education be education by the people, not merely education of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design schooling and pedagogical policy so that they reflect and are accountable to popular/traditional institutions (parliament, marketplace, church, home) rather than being driven solely by specialist elites or experimental cranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically assess 'free' or 'progressive' reforms for hidden coercions
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern 'free' educationists often forbid more things than the old-fashioned educationists; new systems can be as authoritarian as the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize progressive reforms for covert forms of compulsion (e.g., imposing particular play or health regimes). Reforms claiming liberation may still enforce different norms; evaluate deprivations and freedoms in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that informal/social education already exists
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no uneducated people; everyone is educated—often wrongly—by family and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools should not assume a cultural vacuum among the poor or urban children; much harmful or complex culture is absorbed informally. The aim should often be to restore simplicity and counteract precocious or deleterious cultural accretions rather than merely add complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'precedent' heresy: don't lower ideals to fit current mess
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the heresy of precedent to argue that because we have got into a mess we must grow messier to suit it; one should not abandon ideals because reality is imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy responses should not simply conform education or institutions to degraded present conditions. Instead aim to recover or reassert higher ideals (e.g., family tradition) rather than legitimizing current corruptions as norms.
